newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union chief demands progamme of job action.
newsitem.headline: German union chief demands progamme of job action.

text.p: Germany's top trade union official on Monday demanded a wide-ranging programme of job creation measures to ease the country's unemployment numbers, currently riding at a record 4.15 million.

Dieter Schulte, chairman of the DGB Trade Union Federation, told a news conference in Bonn that measures ranging from the reduction of overtime hours to greater investment in public infrastructure projects were necessary.
"There must be progress fast," Schulte said, adding that if such a programme was not put into place this year, a government target of halving unemployment by the year 2000 was at risk.
Schulte said that the industrial base of the former communist-controlled east Germany, where unemployment is disproportionately high, must above all be strengthened.
He declared that the DGB ready, under conditions, to accept more flexible sector-wide wage agreements that would allow individual companies more room to adapt them to their own business conditions.

Schulte however distanced himself from comments made at the weekend by Klaus Zwickel, head of the giant IG Metall metal and engineering union, who argued that quotas for foreign workers were now needed to relieve the German labour market.
Schulte said that in the current jobless situation anything that smacked of xenophobia should be avoided, although he added that Zwickel did not intend any such effect.

German finance minister Theo Waigel, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, has described as "grotesque" the fact that millions of Germans were jobless while so many foreigners worked here.

Schulte's deputy, Ursula Engelen-Kefer, had said in a separate telephone interview on Monday that the union feared that unemployment, which in December rose to 4.15 million, could move to "well over" 4.4 million in January, partly as a result of the poor winter.
Engelen-Kefer said a reduction in overtime hours worked could in itself lead to the creation of some 100,000 new jobs.
She added that the DGB was inviting politicians and employers to a "jobs summit" to be held in April at which possible measures would be discussed.

Engelen-Kefer said that it and other trade unions across Europe would in the next few months making a last-ditch bid to force job creation commitments into the Maastricht Treaty governing European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"The Netherlands presidency runs up to the middle of this year...and it's got to be resolved by then," she said.
All previous attempts by worker groups and left-leaning political bodies to insert specific jobs measures into the Maastricht Treaty have so far proved unsuccessful.
